newsitem.title: USA: Lead scrap merchants watch TV for new sources.
newsitem.headline: Lead scrap merchants watch TV for new sources.

text.p: Let's face it, most lead scrap merchants only think of TV as something to watch after a hard day following prices on the LME.
But a viable new source of lead scrap could be staring them in the face as they settle down in front of the tube.

"TV glass is the area of recycling where opportunities exist to a greater extent," George Gange, general sales manager of Hammond Lead Products, Ind. told delegates at the Institute of Scrap Recycling Industries meeting.

Lead is used in glass for TV tubes to protect viewers from the rays emitted by the cathode. A 19 inch tube contains 3 to 6 pounds of lead oxide, while a 35 inch tube would have about 9 pounds of lead.
And TV sales have risen dramatically over the past 15 years, including computer monitor screens.
Glass makers have become very proficient at recycling tubes broken during manufacture. "As TV sets are scrapped, the tubes have a fair amount of lead that could be recycled."
But one problem is ensuring purity of the scrap for the glass makers to recycle.

Bud DeSart of GNB Technologies, a battery maker and lead recycler, part of Australia's Pacific Dunlop, said a Canadian lead and zinc producer and a major computer company have recently set up a new joint venture to recycle computer monitors in California.
Delegates were also told that the Europeans were ahead in terms of recycling TV tubes to ensure they were not dumped on landfills and possibly leach lead into the ground.
Thomas Parker of Exide Corp, the world's biggest lead battery maker and a major lead recycler, said the company took back some broken glass from Corning for processing to recover lead.
"We can only do this on a limited scale because if we use a lot of it, it slows down the furnace output," Parker said.
